birds.name: House Finch
birds.fact: Native to the West, house finches were released on Long Island in 1940 as pet-shop “Hollywood finches” and spread across the East. Redder males are favored by females.
birds.sndby: Ted Floyd, xeno-canto XC622745, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: American Goldfinch
birds.fact: One of the strictest vegetarians among birds. Goldfinches nest late in summer, when thistle seeds are ripe, and swap bright yellow for olive-brown in winter.
birds.sndby: Will Sweet, xeno-canto XC453934, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Carolina Chickadee
birds.fact: Chickadees hide seeds in many separate spots and can remember where for weeks, then dig them back out when food gets scarce.
birds.sndby: J.R. Rigby, xeno-canto XC309925, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Carolina Wren
birds.fact: Its song sounds like “teakettle, teakettle, teakettle,” and pairs often sing duets. It will nest in odd places: flowerpots, mailboxes, even old boots.
birds.sndby: Jacob Saucier, xeno-canto XC498646, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Tufted Titmouse
birds.fact: Titmice line their nests with hair, and they have been seen plucking it from live raccoons, dogs, and even people.
birds.sndby: Jim Berry, xeno-canto XC649331, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Dark-eyed Junco
birds.fact: Often called “snowbirds” because they show up as winter arrives. The white outer tail feathers flash as they flit away.
birds.sndby: Phoenix Birder, xeno-canto XC563632, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Northern Cardinal
birds.fact: Female cardinals sing too, which is unusual for a North American songbird. During courtship the male feeds her seeds beak to beak.
birds.sndby: David Tattersley, xeno-canto XC1000248, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Pileated Woodpecker
birds.fact: It chisels big rectangular holes in dead wood while hunting carpenter ants. Abandoned holes later shelter owls, ducks and other cavity nesters.
birds.sndby: Mike Nelson, xeno-canto XC102028, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: Fish Crow
birds.fact: It looks just like an American Crow. The giveaway is the voice: a nasal, two-note “uh-uh” instead of a clear “caw.”
birds.sndby: Mike Nelson, xeno-canto XC130581, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0

birds.name: Golden-crowned Kinglet
birds.fact: One of the tiniest songbirds here, yet it survives freezing winter nights by shivering, puffing up its feathers, and huddling with others.
birds.sndby: Mike Nelson, xeno-canto XC135597, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0

birds.name: Eastern Bluebird
birds.fact: Bluebirds nest in tree cavities, and their numbers crashed in the early 1900s when starlings and house sparrows took the holes. Volunteer nest-box trails helped them rebound.
birds.sndby: Robin Carter, xeno-canto XC1374, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: White-throated Sparrow
birds.fact: White-throats come in two color forms, white-striped and tan-striped, and almost always pair with the opposite form. Listen for “Oh-sweet-Canada, Canada, Canada.”
birds.sndby: Matt Wistrand, xeno-canto XC339648, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Red-bellied Woodpecker
birds.fact: The “red belly” is only a faint pink blush you will rarely see. The red cap is the giveaway. Its barbed tongue can reach about two inches past the bill tip.
birds.sndby: Bruce Lagerquist, xeno-canto XC713255, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Ruby-crowned Kinglet
birds.fact: Its ruby crown stays hidden under olive feathers until the male gets excited, then it flares up. A ruby-crowned kinglet flicks its wings constantly.
birds.sndby: Andrew Spencer, xeno-canto XC104679, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: Downy Woodpecker
birds.fact: North America’s smallest woodpecker. It is small enough to forage on thin weed stalks and twigs that bigger woodpeckers can’t cling to.
birds.sndby: Thomas G. Graves, xeno-canto XC89855, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: White-breasted Nuthatch
birds.fact: Nuthatches climb down tree trunks head first. The name comes from “nut-hack”: they wedge a seed into bark and hack it open.
birds.sndby: Andrew Spencer, xeno-canto XC14860, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: Blue Jay
birds.fact: That blue isn’t a pigment. Tiny structures in the feathers scatter light, which is why a crushed blue feather looks brown. Jays also bury acorns and help spread oak trees.
birds.sndby: Christopher McPherson, xeno-canto XC691163, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Cape May Warbler
birds.fact: Its tongue is curled into a tiny tube, a built-in straw for sipping nectar and fruit juice. It nests in northern spruce forests and is named for Cape May, New Jersey, where one of the first specimens was collected.
birds.sndby: Steve Pelikan, xeno-canto XC44424, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: Rusty Blackbird
birds.fact: Rusty Blackbirds have undergone one of the steepest declines of any North American landbird, and scientists are still working out why. They forage in wet woods, flipping leaves along streams.
birds.sndby: Todd Wilson, xeno-canto XC63365, CC BY-NC-ND 2.5

birds.name: Canada Goose
birds.fact: Flying in a V lets geese behind get a lift from the bird in front, and they take turns leading.
birds.sndby: AUDEVARD AurÃ©lien, xeno-canto XC1048808, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: American Crow
birds.fact: Crows remember individual human faces for years, and they seem to pass the grudge along to other crows.
birds.sndby: David Vander Pluym, xeno-canto XC289011, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

birds.name: Northern Flicker
birds.fact: A woodpecker that often feeds on the ground, mainly on ants. Eastern flickers flash bright yellow under the wings and tail when they fly.
birds.sndby: Thomas Magarian, xeno-canto XC354617, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
